comments.author: ubernostrum
comments.text:
tl;dr


Fred Brooks' No Silver Bullet was correct.


No Silver Bullet applies to LLMs the way it applied to other things, and empirical evidence on LLM coding impact sure seems to agree.

You'll get better returns from working on strong software development fundamentals than from forcing all your programmers to use Claude for everything, and that's a repeated message in basically all the major literature.

If LLMs do turn into a revolutionary world-changing silver bullet giving everyone coding superpowers, you'll be able to just adopt them fully when that happens.


The full post is me saying these things much more thoroughly and with citations.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
Great read - thoughtful and nuanced.

I think it underestimates where LLMs can create leverage. My read is that it posits fast-following as an efficient strategy. That's reasonable, but adoption isn't binary - it's a spectrum, and where you sit on it matters a lot.

A couple of moments stood out:


although I'm personally skeptical of the "10x programmer" concept, the software industry overall does seem to accept it as true


I don't think it's universally accepted, but the variance between competent and exceptional engineers can absolutely be that large in practice.


Anecdote time: much of what I've done over my career as a professional programmer is building database-backed web applications and services, and I don't see much of a gain from LLMs… But that capability predates LLMs: Rails' scaffolding, for example, could do it twenty years ago... And not just raw code generation, but also the abstractions available to work with, have progressed to the point where I basically never feel like the raw speed of production of code is holding me back... the majority of my time is spent elsewhere: talking to people who want new software.


The argument that "code generation speed isn't the bottleneck" assumes most engineering time is high-context. In practice, a large portion of the day isn't. It's dependency upgrades, debugging edge-case browser issues, glue code, or chasing down weird inconsistencies. Those tasks are low-context, repetitive, and high-friction - and LLMs are unusually good at them. If that's even 30-50% of the work, the impact is meaningful.

Separately, LLMs don't just increase speed - they change how you explore the solution space and cycle time. I'll often generate multiple approaches in parallel and use them to converge on something better. I've also had end-users vibe-code rough frontends of what they want. These are genuinely useful power tools, not just faster scaffolding.


And though I haven't personally read through the recent alleged leak of the Claude Code source...


I think the Claude Code example is a bit of a red herring. Evaluating an early (and already immensely successful) product in a new paradigm by reading its source is a strange benchmark - especially when iteration speed and product direction matter more than polish at that stage.

comments.author: Student
comments.text:
five-sixths (83%) of time on a “software task” would be spent on things other than coding, which puts a pretty low cap on productivity gains from speeding up just the coding


Ok but to what extent does being able to just generate code replace those other activities?

A lot of “what to build and how” happens because it was cheaper than writing code. Probably 50% of that can be dispensed with by generating prototypes or making parts pluggable.

A lot of communication happens because development needs to be parallelized. If one engineer can write more code (measured by functionality than lines of code) then the need for some of that communication goes away. A lot of the other communication is to avoid integration hell. If rewriting code is cheap the level of agreement needed early in development is reduced. The time it would take to ping pong designs should also be reduced.

What doesn’t go away is testing. What also doesn’t go away is rework. Operating and deploying the software won’t go away directly because of LLMs.

My hunch is that in 10 years organizations that fully embrace the process changes will be shipping about twice as fast. My other hunch is that very few organizations will do that because the bottleneck will be getting high quality information to engineers and actually talking to customers.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
These two parts are more deeply connected then they might seem at first:


the sorts of practices recommended for maximizing LLM-related gains in the DORA report, and in many other similar whitepapers and reports and studies, are or ought to be as fundamental to software development as hand-washing is to surgery.

[...]

When expressing skepticism about LLM coding, a common response is that not adopting it, or even just delaying slightly in adopting it, will inevitably result in being “left behind”, or even stronger effects (for example, words like “obliterated” have been used, more than once, by acquaintances of mine who really ought to know better). LLMs are the future, it’s going to happen whether you like it or not, so get with the program before it’s too late!


Much has been written about the observed bimodal distribution in programmer compensation, where high-skill programmers make something like 5-20x more than low-skill programmers. If you look at what kinds of projects those different groups produce, you'll see a consistent difference: skilled programmers factor big projects into smaller independently-verifiable submodules, write tests that provide good coverage of important branches, and use tooling (static types, linters) to automate trivial verification. Low-skill programmers do few or none of these things, so they spend a lot of time writing cross-cutting changes and then struggling to manually verify whether they're correct.

LLMs introduce a new capability: given a defined scope and a clear goal the computer can independently iterate toward a solution. The properties that make a project easy for humans to reason about (small scope, good tests, quick error ascription) also make LLMs work faster. In a well-maintained codebase an LLM can offload a truly surprising amount of tedious work, which makes skilled developers both more productive and happier -- more thinking, less carpal tunnel.

LLMs also have a new price point, which is the problem. If you are a programmer who can write code as well as an unguided LLM then as of about six months ago your labor is worth less than $0.50/hr. There are a lot of professional programmers out there who do not write code as well as Claude, and it is correct to describe their mid-term career prospects as "obliterated". Their only hope of staying employed as a programmer is to learn how to effectively use LLMs, and they need to be doing it today.


This quote from Brooks:



There is no single development, in either technology or management technique, which by itself promises even a single order-of-magnitude improvement within a decade in productivity, in reliability, in simplicity.



has, I think, been proven wrong by history. Compilers and automatic memory management can both be credited with at least an order of magnitude in all three metrics, not necessarily immediately (early compilers were buggy, early GCs were slow) but over time. If you don't believe me then ask a junior engineer to write a web service in Python and then write it again in x86-64 assembly.

It's still very early in the development of LLMs (ChatGPT was released less than four years ago!), but even now LLMs seem to be at least as effective as compilers when it comes to shifting human attention "up the stack" towards high-level design vs low-level implementation:


Gemma 4 on a three-year-old GPU can fill in simple TODO stub functions while I'm at lunch. I only need to decide on the type signatures.

Gemini Flash can fill in an entire file of TODO stub functions of arbitrary size, and fix any linter/compiler errors that arise, within 30 seconds. I only need to decide on the type signatures of the public API.

Claude can take a brief human-written language spec plus a few examples and turn it into a correct ABNF grammar, then generate test cases guided by that grammar and LCOV.


If this technology doesn't lead to improved productivity in an organization then they're either doing something extremely specialized or their development process is a mess.

But at the same time, your anecdotes about LLM coding all still focus on speed of code generation from a sufficiently well-written and well-designed specification, which once again was not the bottleneck prior to the advent of LLMs.


My experience is that the physical process of writing code (hands on keyboard) is still a significant factor in development speed at most levels of the stack, and that a lot of the non-code process exists as a workaround for the perceived expense of writing code. The only teams for which this doesn't apply are already working at the very highest levels of the abstraction stack (don't need to care about dev time if your stack is Python + Django + TypeScript).

Let's say a company's engineering org works mostly in Java (backend) and Swift (frontend). A new project is estimated by engineering to take two months to a working prototype. Management will pad that to four months, then there will be three months of meetings to decide whether the project is worth attempting and if so which team's budget can fit 320 SWE-hours for the prototype.

If engineering has a particularly capable person assigned to the work then maybe the prototype is completed in one month, of which two weeks were coding and the rest was mixed research/design/debugging. That puts the final ratio at roughly 1/8 coding time, 1/8 thinking, 3/4 bureaucracy.

Claude might reduce the coding time and simplify the research+design time, whatever, even an incredible 50% reduction in dev time would only be 12.5% savings end-to-end. But more importantly it's a coin-operated automaton that operates without human attention, thus no haggling over SWE-hours. You just throw in a few paragraphs of spec and $100 from the department's shared services budget and now you can walk into the first meeting with a kinda-functional prototype.

Instead of three months of meetings you have two weeks, so now you're looking at something like 70% time reduction to first prototype, plus the most expensive part of the process (the meetings) got reduced by 80%. Big savings for Claude!

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
I'm retired; up-thread was what life is like in a corporate environment, the CUDA vs ROCm or data locality stuff is from projects I'm doing for open-source.

Those examples do take up 90% of my time programming. Like, the ideal of programming is I sit down with an idea, type that idea into the computer, and then the final binary springs fully-formed onto my desktop. All the rest of the time is just a consequence of computers having limited hardware capabilities and therefore requiring hand-tuning / optimizations for an acceptable performance.

For example I wanted to try local image generation, community development of which is based around Python frameworks such as PyTorch. However PyTorch requires selection of a particular matrix multiplication backend (CUDA for nVidia, ROCm/HIP for AMD) at build time, and the ROCm build requires a particular version of the ROCm libraries (multiple gigabytes) + a custom LLVM (more gigabytes + takes a long time to build) + the library version has specific requirements about which Linux kernel version is running, because part of the logic apparently lives in the amdgpu driver.

If I skipped that stuff then I would only be able to use the generic CPU driver, which does work but is glacially slow. So for the project to proceed I need to care about GPU drivers minutae.

Another project I'm working on right now is a decompiler, roughly based on Ghidra's decompiler but with more flexible pointer representation (c.f. ghidra#5855). One of the challenges there is the tradeoff between memory management and data locality -- if I use a language like Java or Go with GC then it's very easy to represent the IR as a graph of instructions and operands, but the result is too slow for interactive use on large functions. So I'm writing it in Rust with patterns like "replace pointers with u32 indexes into a Vec<Inst>", and the resulting binary has great performance but the code is way more complicated. Debugging the essential complexity (the individual passes that lift from low-level IR (add, load, cmp, goto) into higher-level structured control flow (ptr_deref_at, for_loop)) takes a lot less time than the accidental complexity (how to represent a partially-transformed CFG while maintaining correctness invariants).

The compression algorithm is because I have another project where I need to keep the data file size down, so it needs to be compressed. The modern choices are zstd and lzma but both of those have their main implementations in C, which means I would need to learn how this language's FFI works. If I choose gzip then the compression ratio is lower but there's already a native implementation available. I could also use WebAssembly as a generic embedding mechanism, but the performance is pretty bad even with the complex JIT runtimes.

This is all accidental complexity. It's tedious and repetitive and it's not what I find enjoyable about programming.

comments.author: Yogthos
comments.text:
The article reads like the author is trying to convince themselves. There's really nothing new here that hasn't been said many times before. The whole argument rests on a false antithesis. To say that because the machine does not do everything by itself, or because it still requires human supervision, it is therefore not useful, is to ignore the whole development of modern software development. Even when the LLM has not sufficient intelligence to carry through an entire process, it may carry through a large number of the nitty-gritty and annoying details involved. It handles syntax quirks, locates library APIs, traces through code, writes boilerplate, and so on. All these things are tedious, and no one ever wants to do them. With an LLM they can be done much more quickly even though the human still makes the final decision.

The author heavily leands on Fred Brooks and the concept of accidental complexity. But they miss the irony entirely. Digging through archaic documentation to find a specific method, or setting up HTTP handlers is the very definition of incidental complexity. Removing that friction allows you to focus on the problem you're actually trying to solve.

In this way the production of software is, in fact, far more accessible. Spending a few months learning how to use an LLM effectively is nothing like spending years learning algorithms, data structures, and design patterns. Building basic programs no longer requires the study of computer science at a level comparable to that of the professional programmer.

comments.author: ubernostrum
comments.text:
To say that because the machine does not do everything by itself, or because it still requires human supervision, it is therefore not useful, is to ignore the whole development of modern software development.


Meanwhile, what I actually wrote was:


Of course, limits on what we can do or gain aren’t necessarily the end of the world. Many of the foundations of computer science, from On Computable Numbers to Rice’s theorem and beyond, place inflexible limits on what we can do, but we still write software nonetheless, and we still work to advance the state of our art. So the No Silver Bullet argument is not the same as arguing that LLMs are necessarily useless, or that no gains can possibly be realized from them. But it is an argument that any gains we do realize are likely going to be incremental and evolutionary, rather than the world-changing revolution many people seem to be expecting.

comments.author: Yogthos
comments.text:
You're right, I forgot about the that bit in the conclusion. My apologies. The dismissive tone of the article was what ultimately stuck in my head when I was writing the comment. Let me address your actual point.

I'd argue the fact that people who've never done software development in their live before can now have an LLM whip up a program for them is already is, in fact, a revolutionary development. This is something that simply wasn't possible just a few years ago. If you weren't a software dev then your options were either to not be able to automate something or pay thousands of dollars for a developer to do it.

I can give you a concrete example here. I have a friend who was a Windows user. He's a designer and always found Linux to be too intimidating to switch over to. I helped him get set up with DeepSeek and opencode, and he's been able to solve every problem he's run into using the tool. If he doesn't know how to do something on Linux, or he needs to figure out why something isn't working, or make a script, the LLM solves the problem for him. He's been using Linux for about half a year now without any complaints. For him, this is a revolutionary thing, as he was able to make a jump to Linux which was simply not worth doing before.

Of course, the LLM can't write large scale software on its own, and you need humans in the loop for that. But even there, I'd argue the changes are revolutionary as well. For example, I've never worked with frontend development using Js. I had to work with React and build a frontend recently for a non-trivial app. This is something I just wouldn't have been able to do previously. I know how to structure applications, what good architecture looks like, and so on. But I simply don't have the experience with the specific stack, I don't know the language quirks, the libraries, or the tooling. This would've been months of work to internalize previously. The LLM papered right over all that for me. I was able to use Js just as easily as the languages I'm well versed in. Externalizing experience that used to take many months, or years to develop, into a tool is absolutely revolutionary.

I also disagree with the claim that the limitations of LLMs require some sort of a breakthrough to overcome. The approach may simply lie in better tooling. We already have languages that allow doing formal proofs and contracts. It could be that we simply move in that direction. The human writes a declarative spec for the functionality they want, and the LLM has to figure out how to fill that spec. You can encode whatever requirements you want into the contract, and simply treat the LLM generation as you would a genetic algorithm converging on a solution. People are already starting to do this in ad hoc way with forcing LLMs to do TDD. This would again be a revolutionary leap akin to going from writing assembly to using a high level language.

comments.text: Since this leans on the DORA report quite a bit, it's important to point out that the DORA report's survey was collected from June 13 to July 21, 2025. While that technically falls over the release of Claude Code, it did not fully achieve widespread adoption yet. It will be interesting to see what future reports indicate.

comments.author: ubernostrum
comments.text:
While that technically falls over the release of Claude Code, it did not fully achieve widespread adoption yet. It will be interesting to see what future reports indicate.


There is a paragraph in my post which begins:


The usual response to reports like these is to claim they’re based on people using older LLMs, and the models coming out now are the truly revolutionary ones, which won’t have any of those problems.


I refer you to what follows.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:
if the people claiming “this time is the world-changing revolutionary leap, for sure” were wrong all the prior times they said that (as they have to have been, since if any prior time had actually been the revolutionary leap they wouldn’t need to say this time will be), why should anyone believe them this time?


The problem there is that you risk bundling too wide of a group of people together.

In the case or Claude Code and Opus 4.5+ (the November set of models) there are a notable number of voices who did NOT previously say "this time is world-changing" about previous model improvements, who are now saying that these coding agents are genuinely useful when they were skeptical before.

My favorite example is this one by Paul Ford.

comments.author: ubernostrum
comments.text:
I linked that Paul Ford article from my post. I also think it's actually a really strong argument for my position.

Back when that article first went up, I posted on social media (initially on Mastodon, but cross-posted to Bluesky where I know you follow me), about how nothing in that article really felt new or groundbreaking to me: that quick data converter is the kind of thing I used to do at the Journal-World back in the day, and that you used to do, too. We could quickly bang out these kinds of projects already, twenty-plus years ago.

Paul Ford's analysis of how long it would take and how much it would cost to do a bespoke data converter at his former company isn't based on the time or cost of producing code, it's based on delivering that software in a different environment, where that project has to be justified and prioritized and documented and have a spec and acceptance criteria and a testing plan and all the other bits.

To go back to the story I posted on Mastodon/Bluesky: if I went to the teams I work with today and showed them the same crime data set the reporter brought down to me in the News Center basement twenty years ago and asked them to build the same online feature for it, the coding time for it would probably be a little bit faster, thanks to advances in tools over the years. But the project would need to be thought through, and prioritized against other projects competing for resources, and have a specification written, and acceptance criteria, and a testing plan, and all the other bits. It would take a lot longer than two days. But the coding, even if done 100% by hand by humans, would still go very quickly. What wouldn't go quickly, and what an LLM can't make go quickly, is all the other bits.

And as much as it would feel great to just go off and build whatever I feel like building whenever I feel like it, I know from experience that in most environments having processes is important, even if it thwarts me on occasion. For example: there's a project at my day job that I've wanted to get built for a while. Writing the code is maybe an hour or two of work, without involving an LLM. I don't need any help prototyping it, I know exactly how it needs to work, and I've built things like it before. The sticking point is that it would replace a pretty critical existing component that a whole bunch of things rely on, and replacing that requires notifying and getting buy-in from a lot of people, and a migration plan, and a fallback plan, and coordinating the switchover with people watching to make sure it goes smoothly, and... well, it doesn't matter how much faster I could write that code with an LLM. An LLM could literally magically reduce the coding time to zero and still not make much of a meaningful dent in the overall end-to-end time to deliver the project, because the coding is not the bottleneck.

It's also not the bottleneck for Paul Ford. He knows that. You know that. I know you both know that.

comments.text: I primarily wanted to provide that context, because for a reader of that post the observation period of the DORA report was not mentioned.

comments.author: gerikson
comments.text:
Great piece. Summarizes alot of the things I have been thinking about.

Specifically, this piece and people like @simonw consistently promote the idea of stuff like testing, CI, etc. - the software equivalent of surgeons scrubbing before an operation. But I think that a lot of software development today is done even without that, and adding LLMs into that mix won't be helpful - it might even be negative.

Software shops with good "hygiene" will probably get  a modest boost in productivity from LLMs, but they're already a lot more productive than shops without hygiene.
